abstract: With rare exceptions, progressive movements consider philanthropy conservative. This article identifies why and outlines the praxis of movement-led philanthropy as developed and practiced by women-led feminist resource-mobilizing funders in response to these concerns. The article identifies five ways that philanthropy is implicated in structural injustice and undermines efforts to take on structural injustice. Even the critical trends within the political theory of philanthropy focus on institutions over practices; our argument uses a feminist grounded normative theory methodology to study organizations whose existences were born out of concerns with philanthropy’s power. Women’s social movements created resource-mobilizing philanthropic funders that developed practices specifically designed to address the injustices of philanthropy and to maintain support for movements and advocacy. We study four such organizations: Fundo Elas (ELAS + ) (Brazil), Mongolian Women’s Fund (MONES) (Mongolia), Reconstruction Women’s Fund (RWF) (Serbia), and Women’s Fund Tanzania (WFT) (Tanzania). Their practices are foundational to a social movement-led praxis of philanthropy that endeavors to change the power dynamics of philanthropy. The critique of the power of philanthropy, combined with a grounded account of practices reshaping philanthropy’s power from within, yields a movement-led praxis of philanthropy.
title: Funding Justice: Movement-led philanthropy

abstract: This paper uses high-frequency administrative data to show that most U.S. workers experience substantial month-to-month fluctuations in pay, even within ongoing employment relationships. Monthly earnings instability is pervasive but is masked in annual data. Moreover, this instability is unequally distributed: lower-income, hourly workers face more instability than higher-income, salaried workers. Firm-driven fluctuations in hours account for a large share of this instability. Monthly earnings instability, in turn, increases spending volatility and job separations. Short-term earnings risk is therefore a significant feature of the labor market and falls disproportionately on the most financially fragile workers.
title: Earnings Instability

abstract: Like other colonial powers, Belgium enacted pro-birth policies in its colony starting in the 1920s. We investigate their impacts on women who grew up in colonial Congo, using individual fertility outcomes for a sample of 30,000 women. Given that Catholic nuns implemented these policies, we exploit temporal and geographic heterogeneity in exposure to different types of missions, Catholic, Catholic with nuns and Protestants. We find that Catholic nuns succeeded in stimulating fertility, unlike other missionaries. We investigate mechanisms and show that Catholic female education – and its promotion of domesticity – played a decisive role. Finally, we find modest traces on fertility today.
title: A mandate to multiply: the effects of pro-birth policies on fertility in colonial Congo

abstract: Local ethnic amenities can foster the growth of immigrant enclaves, affecting economic and cultural integration. We study the centralized placement of “ethnic” Catholic churches in the United States during the Age of Mass Migration (1900-1930), focusing on Polish and Italian immigrants. Polish immigrants relied more heavily on the local parish to organise communal life. Following the opening of a Polish (but not Italian) church, co-ethnic residents experienced declines in occupation-based earnings but strengthened communal ties, measured by in-group marriage and naming, relative to matched neighbourhoods. These effects persist into the second generation and are not observed among other local residents, including Jews and non-Polish Catholics.
title: Enclaves and Assimilation in the Age of Mass Migration: Evidence from Ethnic Catholic Churches

abstract: Empirical stylized facts in the literature concerning “sin” versus “angel” stocks display marked asymmetries in investor behavior. Through a set of experiments, we examine whether such biases can be micro-founded via individuals’ preferences and belief formations. With respect to portfolio allocation decisions, we find that the responses to negative environmental and social externalities are several times larger in magnitude than their responses to comparable positive externalities, ceteris paribus. Negative externalities also modestly increase pessimism about future investment performance, whereas positive externalities have little discernible effect on beliefs. This asymmetry is pervasive across our sample, exhibits heterogeneity across individuals, and is comparable to or greater in magnitude than estimates observed in loss aversion analyses. These findings help rationalize several existing stylized empirical facts documented in the responsible investing literature and carry implications for the growing body of theoretical work modeling the role of nonpecuniary investor preferences in asset pricing. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06826 .

title: The Asymmetry in Responsible Investing Preferences and Beliefs

abstract: The 0-1 knapsack problem is a fundamental problem of discrete choice that permeates many diverse fields and applications, but relatively little is known about what instances human solvers find more difficult than others. This paper reports the results of the first large-scale randomized controlled field experiment investigating this question, conducted in partnership with a global mobile gaming platform. A total of 100,000 different knapsack instances were predesigned for this study and randomly assigned to each player attempt at the knapsack problem. For our base-case analysis, there were 17,950,838 distinct player accounts who made a total of 150,284,195 submitted solution attempts. Contrary to expectations, players performed better on problems that were rated as more difficult by two traditional measures of knapsack difficulty (the Pearson correlation between value and weight vectors and Sahni complexity), but performed worse on problem instances that featured large optimality gaps from a suite of heuristic solution algorithms. These suggest that optimality gaps can serve as promising measures of human-perceived knapsack difficulty and potentially could be used to measure human-perceived problem difficulty for other types of discrete choice problems. We found evidence that players improved their performance with repeated attempts at the knapsack task overall, but less-experienced players of the mobile game improved more quickly than more-experienced players. Through the construction of a new measure of human-perceived difficulty rating for each knapsack instance, we found evidence that players who were assigned to instances with a higher difficulty rating in the past tended to perform better on future attempts. This paper was accepted by Manel Baucells, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: S. Agarwal’s research is supported by the Ministry of Education, Singapore, under its Social Science and Humanities Research Thematic [Grant SSRC2024-SSHRTG-022] and the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72495154]. J. Goh’s research is supported by a Startup [Grant R-314-000-110-133] and a 2021 Humanities and Social Sciences Faculty Research Fellowship from the National University of Singapore. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.00747 .

abstract: This paper examines how new entrants influenced content strategies in the U.S. online political news business from 2014 to 2021. Using a novel measure of article opinionation that captures the extent to which an article displays editorializing and persuasive language, we provide correlational evidence that new entrants produce articles that are more opinionated than those of incumbents, even when reporting on the same event. We then show that there is an economic rationale for this content strategy: opinionated articles receive more engagement on Twitter, and this engagement translates to increased webpage visits, crucial for advertising revenue. Consistent with these incentives, we provide evidence that news providers increase the average opinion level in their articles in response to competition and advertiser pressure. These shifts are accompanied by a possibly unintended consequence: opinionated content is associated with greater anger and hate speech in social media engagement. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01487 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Opinion Trumps Fact: Entry and Competition in Online Political News

abstract: We analyze novel data on corporate contributions to ballot initiatives at the U.S. state level. Firms make large contributions to ballot measure campaigns in favor of or against specific initiatives. They contribute significantly more to business initiatives compared with ideological initiatives. Corporate campaign spending is systematically associated with the likelihood that a ballot measure passes. Contributing firms experience changes in sales growth following the passage of important ballot measures. Following successful (failed) initiatives, all firms in affected industries exhibit significantly more positive (negative) cumulative abnormal returns around the election, but contributing firms do more so than peers. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: R. Fahlenbrach gratefully acknowledges financial support from the Swiss Finance Institute. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06801 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Corporate Contributions to Ballot Measure Campaigns: Real Effects and Valuation

abstract: We study a setting in which personal acquisition of information is costly and maintaining personal contacts to share information socially is also costly. The theory predicts star networks, with small groups sustaining an active hub and large groups allowing in addition for an inactive hub equilibrium. Experiments with small (8 subjects) and large (50 subjects) groups show star-like networks throughout. In small groups, behavior matches the active hub prediction. In large groups, hubs are inactive or engage in activity far in excess of the active hub equilibrium depending on how much information subjects are given on their own and others’ earnings. The hub’s activity level shapes relative earnings of subjects and the overall performance of the group. This paper was accepted by Roberto Weber, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: This work was supported by H2020 Future and Emerging Technologies [IBSEN Contract 662725]; the Keynes Fund, University of Cambridge; and the Creative-Pioneering Researchers Program, Seoul National University. S. Goyal acknowledges financial support from the Center of Behavioural Institutional Design and Tamkeen [New York University Abu Dhabi Research Institute Award CG005]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07308 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Connectors and Influencers

abstract: Some organizations provide employees with feedback on the demographics of people they have chosen to spotlight, hire, and promote, hoping to spur more diverse future selections. However, it is an open question whether purely descriptive feedback accomplishes this. We theorize and show that descriptive feedback highlighting low past selection rates of women or racial minorities (e.g., “5% of previous experts interviewed were women”) triggers a motivation to respond without prejudice, increasing the subsequent selection of members of underrepresented groups. Conversely, providing descriptive feedback about low selection rates of people with other attributes (e.g., areas of expertise, geographical location) that do not evoke image or reputational concerns has less influence on future decisions. We demonstrate these patterns across seven preregistered experiments (total n = 6,502), including one framed field experiment (Study 2). One study identifies motivation to respond without prejudice as a mediator of the effect of descriptive feedback about past choices on future selections of women and racial minorities. Another study shows that when women are overrepresented, the effect of descriptive feedback reverses in direction, increasing the subsequent selection of men (due to concerns about fairness), but this effect is significantly smaller in magnitude than the feedback effect produced when women are underrepresented. Practically, the effects of descriptive feedback were 45%–80% as large as simulating a strict quota requiring that at least one woman or racial minority be selected for a given opportunity, highlighting that descriptive feedback is a light-touch but potentially powerful intervention for promoting diversity. This paper was accepted by George Wu, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01479 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Does Feedback Enhance Diversity in Selection Decisions?

abstract: Dans le monde financier moderne, chaque institution a pour raison d’être d’instaurer et de préserver la confiance au sein de la société. Cet article soutient que l’intelligence artificielle fait peser de nouvelles menaces sur cette confiance, susceptibles de mettre fondamentalement en péril le système financier. Les « deepfakes » et le clonage vocal rendent difficile la vérification de l’identité ou la fiabilité des preuves visuelles et audio. Une autre menace réside dans l’asymétrie de compréhension, les agents d’IA agissant selon des règles décisionnelles et des représentations du monde que les humains ne peuvent ni interpréter ni contrôler. Les politiques doivent s’adapter pour préserver la responsabilité, renforcer la résilience face à la fraude facilitée par l’IA et protéger la confiance institutionnelle.
title: La confiance au-delà du contact en face à face : l’IA et l’avenir de la finance

abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) reduces the time and effort required to prepare competitive research proposals, potentially reshaping the allocation of agricultural research funding. We study these implications in the context of the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA)'s Agriculture and Food Research Initiative (AFRI), the primary federal mechanism supporting U.S. agricultural research and innovation. Using a formal economic model of the AFRI grant market developed from a no‐AI benchmark, we analyse two AI scenarios: independent adoption , in which AI use is uncorrelated with researcher quality, and correlated adoption . AI‐driven reductions in preparation costs can increase submissions from marginal projects, weaken peer‐review signal informativeness and amplify institutional funding advantages even when underlying research quality is comparable. Allowing AI adoption to correlate with researcher quality shows that compensatory adoption—a negative adoption–quality correlation deepens signal degradation, whereas the correlation must exceed approximately 0.10 before fixed‐pool informativeness improves relative to the no‐AI benchmark. In the calibration, uniform high adoption increases equilibrium submissions by 18.0%. Under a heterogeneous scenario in which 70% of potential investigators receive high‐intensity AI assistance and 30% receive none, submissions increase by 6.2%, while mean funded quality falls by 3.5%. These allocative effects coexist with proposal preparation resource savings. We evaluate second‐best responses implementable within USDA's existing authority, including mandatory pre‐proposals, meritorious‐pool lotteries, AI‐use disclosure and targeted AI‐access programmes for historically Black land‐grant and other minority‐serving institutions. Generative AI can therefore raise applicant productivity while weakening the information and selection mechanisms underlying efficient and equitable research funding.
title: When Grant Writing Becomes Cheap: Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Efficiency of Agricultural Research Funding

abstract: Shadow prices from large-scale energy system optimization models (ESOMs) are widely used as long-term electricity price proxies in research and policy analysis. While their structural limitations are broadly acknowledged, no systematic empirical evidence exists on their reliability as market price proxies. We address this gap with a novel three-stage statistical framework (Kruskal–Wallis tests, t -tests, Pearson correlations) applied to ENTSO-E day-ahead prices and shadow prices from GENeSYS-MOD — one illustrative example among many cost-minimising ESOMs — across 22 European countries and four temporal resolutions. We find that shadow prices are compressed relative to observed market prices across all temporal resolutions. Volatility compression is most pronounced at the day-of-week level ( 10 × on average) and at the hour-of-day level ( 7 × on average). Month-of-year and season resolutions show smaller but still substantial compression (3– 4 × on average). Despite this, day-of-week, month-of-year, and season price patterns are structurally aligned with ENTSO-E observations. Hour-of-day alignment improves with model year but the observed market pattern is structurally shifting, making it the resolution hardest to use reliably. Independent literature projections from other LP-based models fall in the same compressed range, indicating that compression is a model-class property rather than a single-model artefact; direct empirical validation across other ESOM families remains an open task. Addressing these structural limitations is a promising avenue for future model development. In the interim, we propose resolution-conditional guidelines to support more principled shadow price applications.
title: Can shadow prices from energy system optimization models serve as reliable electricity price indicators?

abstract: The intersection of environmental policies and trade policies on external diseconomies has received considerable attention in recent years. However, the impacts of the timing or sequencing of environmental policy instruments have received little attention, and especially pollution taxes versus import tariffs as instruments of environmental policy on economic performance have not been formally considered. This forms the focus of this work. In a political economy context, import tariffs might be imposed first due to protectionist or budgetary considerations, while environmental compulsions might lead to precedence of pollution taxes. Our results, using a modeling framework where goods across trading nations emit pollution in both production and consumption, show that social welfare, producer surplus, and consumer surplus are greater, and both pollution taxes and import tariffs are lower when the decision of import tariffs precedes that of pollution taxes, as opposed to the alternative sequencing putting pollution taxes ahead of tariffs.
title: The sequencing of import tariffs and emissions taxes: Does the timing impact economic performance?

abstract: This study investigates the impact of artificial intelligence on urban carbon-emission efficiency, addressing the limited empirical evidence on its environmental effects in the existing literature. Using panel data from Chinese cities covering the period 2011–2023, this paper employs a fixed-effects model to examine the relationship between artificial intelligence development and carbon-emission efficiency. The results show that artificial intelligence significantly improves the efficiency of reducing urban carbon emissions. Mechanism analyses further indicate that artificial intelligence enhances carbon-emission efficiency by stimulating green technological innovation, upgrading industrial structure, and accelerating the development of the digital economy. In addition, the effect is stronger in non-old industrial cities, resource-based cities, and regions with stronger intellectual property protection and higher levels of human capital. These findings provide new insights into the environmental implications of artificial intelligence and offer important policy implications for promoting low-carbon transition and sustainable urban development.

abstract: Following the 2008 food price crisis, West African governments adopted National Rice Development Strategies (NRDS) to strengthen domestic rice value chains. Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire, two neighbouring countries with similar rice sectors and a shared history of large-scale State-led intervention, have since followed diverging paths. Côte d’Ivoire has carried its agro-industrial vision into the pole leader policy, whereas Ghana has redirected support towards the traditional value chain, combining supply-side and demand-side instruments. We explain this contrast through the Advocacy Coalition Framework, drawing on content analysis of 68 semi-structured interviews triangulated with grey literature and on a cluster analysis of stakeholder beliefs. In Côte d’Ivoire, a dominant coalition controls a policy process marked by restricted forums and the absence of brokers, sustaining “zombie ideas”. In Ghana, open forums, policy brokers and a coalition of civil society organisation enabled contending beliefs to reshape policy. The comparison shows how the openness of policy subsystems conditions change, and highlights the enduring tension between food security and self-sufficiency.
title: Policy change and continuity in food security policy: Examining advocacy coalitions in Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire’s rice sector

abstract: This paper studies how the statutory right to work part-time affects mothers’ post-birth labor market outcomes exploiting administrative data. The identification is based on a reform in Germany that introduced for the first time a general legal entitlement for employees to work part-time. I find that the reform increased the probability of eligible mothers working part-time in the short run after childbirth, indicating that the law relaxed a binding constraint. The reform had positive effects on mothers’ employment and labor income in the longer run. The latter is partly due to a higher job continuity among eligible mothers.
title: Does the right to work part-time affect mothers’ labor market outcomes?

abstract: We examine teacher-level cellphone permissiveness in a setting where phones are often used for instructional support and teachers retain discretion over classroom cellphone use. Using linked Chilean administrative and survey data, we exploit variation in cellphone policy within teachers across cohorts and within students across subjects. Greater restrictiveness modestly reduces eighth graders’ cellphone use in class, but not tenth graders’. It also lowers eighth graders’ self-perceived academic capability, with no detectable effects on test scores. These findings inform settings, more common in low- and middle-income countries, involving uneven classroom enforcement within schools and where phones serve as low-cost instructional tools.
title: The consequences of cellphone restrictions in classrooms

abstract: Antitrust agencies face an organizational trade-off. Local offices may preserve geographically embedded information, whereas centralized teams can pool scarce personnel and expertise for complex cases. We study this trade-off in the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) Antitrust Division’s 2013 reorganization, which closed four of seven field offices, reassigned 23 states and territories, and concentrated enforcement resources in the remaining locations. Using a balanced panel of U.S. public firms from 2010 through 2016 and a difference-in-differences design, we find that markups for firms in reassigned jurisdictions fell by 0.038 to 0.072 relative to firms whose field-office coverage did not change; the smaller estimate, obtained with industry-by-year fixed effects, is significant at the 10% level. The decline is concentrated among firms with the highest initial markups and is strongest when product-market rivalry overlaps former office jurisdictions; profitability and TNIC-based concentration show corresponding upper-tail declines. The distance gradient is consistent with local information conditioning the gains from consolidation. Among high-markup firms, the markup decline is largest when reassignment entails a small distance increase and attenuate monotonically as the closure-induced increase in distance grows. Together, the evidence indicates that the reorganization was followed by declines in market-power outcomes concentrated among initially high-markup firms. These patterns are consistent with proximity moderating the effects of consolidation.
title: Antitrust Enforcement and Market Power: Evidence from DOJ Field-Office Closures

abstract: This paper investigates the role of mortgage market concentration in the propagation mechanism of micro-level shocks and macroeconomic effects. First, we document substantial concentration in the U.S. mortgage market between 1990 and 2020. Second, we find that lender-specific mortgage supply fluctuations affect aggregate mortgage, house price, and employment dynamics using a Granular Instrumental Variable approach (Gabaix and Koijen, 2024). The larger the idiosyncratic shocks to newly issued mortgages, the stronger the mortgage, house price, and employment growth. Third, we show that despite comparable—or even higher—within-market concentration, granularity effects from the shadow banking sector are substantially weaker than those from traditional banks. We trace this differential to the distinction between two dimensions of market structure: shadow banks are at least as dominant as traditional banks within individual metropolitan areas, but are far more geographically diversified across markets, diluting the local impact of any given idiosyncratic shock.
title: Granular shocks and shadow banks: Concentration and real effects in mortgage markets

abstract: We study how fiscally backed credit interventions affect the transmission of monetary policy using detailed credit registry data from Brazil. Government direct credit partially insulates loan rates and credit quantities from monetary policy shocks, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises. Government-subsidized (earmarked) credit interacts with lending relationships to shape pass-through, which is strongest among more dependent clients and in less competitive markets, consistent with a relationship-based hold-up mechanism. Overall, government credit stabilizes credit supply and supports targeted borrowers but weakens the aggregate transmission of monetary policy and generates heterogeneous effects across credit market segments.
title: The nuanced role of government credit in monetary policy transmission

abstract: The United States experienced two major demographic ’booms’ during the second half of the twentieth century, in births after 1945 and in divorces 25 years later. This paper argues that the two booms are linked. As the baby-boomers were entering marriageable age, men in previous cohorts were faced with exceptionally good remarriage prospects. I find that across states people in the pre-boom generations were more likely to have ever divorced the bigger the relative supply of young women (instrumenting the size of the baby-boom with WWII mobilization rates). I construct a simple dynamic marriage and remarriage model (matched to the pre-1970s matching patterns) that illustrates how age-gap preferences can translate a cohort-size variation into a rise in divorce.
title: The baby boom and the US divorce boom

abstract: Digital goods generate substantial consumer welfare, but their valuations are difficult to estimate because many are free to consumers. We investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can reconstruct these valuations over time using incentive-compatible binary choice experiments. We benchmark predictions against eight waves of representative US survey data collected between 2016 and 2024. Calibrating GPT-4-Turbo on one year, we find that it approximates the magnitude and temporal patterns of median human valuations in other years. Newer models do not necessarily improve predictions, tending to favor monetary compensation. Our findings suggest opportunities and limitations for longitudinal valuations using LLMs.
title: LLM Time Machines: Valuing digital goods over time

abstract: We study the effect of migration on firms’ capital deepening, leveraging a massive influx of immigrant workers with varying skill sets from Venezuela and Haiti in Chile between 2015 and 2019. Using a theoretical framework that allows for differential productivity between native and immigrant workers, we estimate how firm capital responds to increases in the supply of skilled and unskilled workers. Identification relies on the shift-share instrument to estimate firms’ exposure to immigration shocks. We use unique employer-employee data to match worker characteristics, including country of origin and education level, to balance sheet data from firms’ tax returns, providing highly detailed information about the labor composition and capital in the firm that is not available in other contexts. Our findings show that a 1 p.p. increase in the proportion of skilled immigrants relative to total skilled workers in the firm raises firms’ capital per worker by 1 to 2%. The impact of skilled labor on capital deepening is nonlinear and declines as firms’ immigrant concentration increases, consistent with our model’s predictions. This nonlinear relationship is driven by the imperfect substitutability between immigrants and native workers within the same skill group.
title: Immigrants' skills and capital deepening: evidence from Chile

abstract: Farming systems in many parts of Australia are increasingly crop dominant with crops often intensively managed. In a key grain‐producing region of Australia, we investigate when and where it is optimal to apply a fungicide on cereal crops with moderate susceptibility to a foliar fungal pathogen controllable by fungicide. A state‐contingent framework is novelly applied to identify the optimal use of a fungicide in cereal crops at three locations with different production environments, under the management objectives of profit maximisation or utility maximisation. Results show that the nature and value of the crop, the farm location, the cost of the fungicide and the state‐contingent nature of the decision environment greatly affect decisions concerning when fungicide applications are financially most desirable. The use of fungicide is more profitable in higher rainfall, higher yielding locations. Optimal responses under profit maximisation or utility maximisation are identical for the contingent states, crops and locations examined. Depending on farm location and crop type, the fungicide spray decision can be simple or quite nuanced. We conclude there is merit in embedding the state‐contingent framework in a farm management decision aid.
journal: Australian Journal of Agricultural and Resource Economics
title: When to Apply Fungicide: A State Contingent Analysis

abstract: Payers increasingly use competitive tendering to reduce expenditures on patent‐protected pharmaceuticals. Using a duopoly model with horizontally differentiated drugs, we show that tendering can harm patients and fail to reduce costs. When demand depends on physicians' tolerance for treatment loss, tendering yields a mixed‐strategy equilibrium: firms balance bidding low to win the contract against bidding high to exploit residual demand. Compared with decentralized competition, tendering worsens patient outcomes and increases expected prices unless the treatment‐loss tolerance is sufficiently high. Quality asymmetries and captive segments further amplify these distortions, highlighting critical trade‐offs in procurement design.
title: Winning the prescription: competitive tenders versus decentralized competition

abstract: Land abandonment is a persistent and uneven process reshaping rural Europe, with risks for biodiversity, land degradation, and rural socio-cultural and economic resilience. Although it is often framed as a negative condition to be reversed, we argue in this Viewpoint that land abandonment can be approached as a window for change, which in some contexts can take a more transformative form. We put forward four alternative pathways to help understand and strategically shape responses to land abandonment in Europe: sustainable land management; heritage and identity; community and social innovation; and rewilding and nature. To support comparison across pathways, we adapt the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) transformative change framework to make explicit how interventions frame abandonment, their intent for change, and the alignment they mobilise across visions, institutions and practices, including implications for equity, power and decision-making. Drawing on illustrative responses, we suggest that many initiatives prioritise coping or adaptation, while transformative elements tend to sit in specific governance and instrument choices rather than system-wide shifts. Transformative change, where pursued, should therefore be treated as one end of a spectrum rather than a default expectation and requires explicit intent, durable institutional anchoring and legitimacy. The paper offers a heuristic perspective — not a definitive typology of existing approaches — to help planning and policy debates become clearer about aims and limits, better able to match instruments to intent, and more attentive to the governance and distributional conditions under which responses endure, evolve or become contested.
title: Land abandonment as a window for transformative change: Response pathways in Europe

abstract: This paper examines the impact of credit constraints on rural households’ climate resilience in Togo, with a focus on the roles of land ownership and institutional quality. Using nationally representative household data and an endogenous switching regression approach, the analysis accounts for selection bias and the endogeneity of credit access. Results indicate that households facing credit constraints, whether global, demand-side, or supply-side, exhibit significantly lower adaptive capacity. Secure land tenure mitigates the negative impact of credit constraints relative to non-ownership, although this buffering effect is weaker for female landowners than for male landowners, indicating that ownership alone does not fully protect women from constraint-related resilience losses. Institutional quality further shapes resilience, as households in contexts with strong perceptions of corruption control and respect for the rule of law are better able to adapt. Treatment effect estimates confirm that the losses in resilience associated with credit constraints are substantial and causal. Policy implications highlight the need for integrated interventions combining rural credit expansion, land tenure security, gender-sensitive support, and institutional reforms to strengthen inclusive climate adaptation and sustainable rural development.
title: Dealing with credit constraints for households' climate resilience: the role of land ownership and institutional quality in Togo

abstract: Urban expansion into natural floodplains has reduced retention capacity across Europe, increasing downstream flood exposure and creating dependence on engineered substitutes such as dry retention basins. These basins are frequently sited on private agricultural land, producing a structural tension: they deliver public flood protection while concentrating hydrological, agronomic, and economic costs on a small group of landholders. How this tension unfolds – and whether governance frameworks adequately address it – remains poorly understood, particularly in peri-urban catchments where development pressure, climate extremes, and agricultural livelihoods intersect. This paper analyses the mechanisms through which progressive floodplain occupation generates and redistributes flood risk, using a two-century land-use reconstruction (~1820–2024), official hydraulic modelling results (Q10, Q100, Q500 scenarios), and qualitative interviews with land users in the Glinščica catchment (Ljubljana, Slovenia), centred on the Brdnikova dry retention basin. Results reveal a pronounced transition from agricultural floodplain to heavily urbanised catchment, with built-up land increasing more than fifteenfold, primarily at the expense of arable land and meadows in low-elevation zones. Inundation under moderate return periods recurrently affects valley-bottom agricultural soils, where farmers report sediment deposition, soil compaction, invasive species pressure, yield losses, and increased labour demands. Recently introduced compensation mechanisms address direct crop damage, but cumulative and indirect impacts remain uncovered. The findings indicate that dry retention basins in peri-urban agricultural settings are best understood as engineered flood-retention infrastructure embedded in multifunctional agricultural land use, rather than as full ecological-restoration measures. They require integrated governance frameworks that anticipate distributional effects, ensure equitable compensation, and coordinate spatial planning with agricultural and environmental policy. Given the single-case design, the study advances context-sensitive governance considerations relevant to comparable peri-urban retention settings.
title: Land-use change and flood-risk governance in a peri-urban catchment of Ljubljana, Slovenia

abstract: Using a dose–response framework, we re-evaluate the 1918 Influenza Pandemic and its impact on educational attainment and occupation score across geographies in the United States. Our sample covers over 1800 counties in 35 states. We estimate that the 1918 Influenza had limited impact on long-run outcomes. We find different effects in rural and urban locations, with the urban net effect of the flu close to zero for educational attainment and occupational outcomes. Our estimates diverge from the prior literature due to differences in our linked sample and measure of flu intensity. Finally, we find suggestive evidence that fetal selection is a potential mechanism that partially explains why our estimates differ.
title: 1918 Influenza pandemic across America - New evidence using county-level data

abstract: This paper estimates the policy and economic impacts of a European Union-led effort to review and “blacklist” jurisdictions based on their noncompliance with international standards designed to curb corporate profit shifting and private tax evasion. Using a combination of regression discontinuity and difference-and-difference methods, I find evidence of improvements in tax governance four years after the inception of the list. However, despite evidence that some jurisdiction raised their tax rates in response to the listing exercise, there no clear evidence that listing had a significant impact on offshore wealth or shifted profits, largely because the bulk of jurisdictions that host both of these were not targeted by the EU. The results suggest that “coercive” efforts to reduce global tax evasion and avoidance will struggle without better targeting and enforcement.
title: The impact of tax blacklisting

abstract: This study conducted two natural field experiments in Yokohama City, Japan, to evaluate the effectiveness of behavioral nudges in promoting automatic debit registration for property tax payments. While much of the existing literature on tax compliance focuses on reminder letters and other communications, relatively little attention has been paid to payment method choice, even though payment methods may affect both administrative costs and taxpayers’ recurring compliance burdens. In the first experiment, a combined intervention consisting of a nudge flyer and the owner code required for the application increased the probability of applying for automatic debit by 8.8% points. In the second experiment, which separately varied these components, the nudge flyer and the inclusion of the owner code increased the application probability by 2.7 and 2.8% points, respectively. Despite the increase in automatic debit adoption, we find no evidence that these interventions improve on-time payment within the time frame observed in our experiments. This may reflect limited scope for large aggregate improvements given the baseline level of on-time payment, or the possibility that the interventions primarily affected taxpayers who would have paid on time even in the absence of automatic debit. Taken together, our findings highlight both the potential and the limits of behavioral nudges in improving tax administration outcomes.
title: Nudging automatic debit for property tax: evidence from two natural field experiments

abstract: Firms’ access to external finance differs widely across Europe. This column uses data from the ECB’s Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises to map these differences and to study what they mean for monetary policy. The authors find that countries in which firms face tighter financial frictions respond less to the ECB’s monetary policy changes, and that they face a worse trade-off between output and inflation. A model of the monetary union suggests that financial integration in the spirit of the Savings and Investments Union would make monetary policy more effective, but potentially at a cost to financial stability.
title: The geography of financial frictions

abstract: Raising educational attainment is the canonical way skills keep pace with technology. This column argues that changes in learning content matter just as much, drawing on five decades of legally binding German vocational training curricula linked to patents and administrative worker records. Occupational curricula more exposed to digital technologies are rewritten faster, mainly by adding new skills rather than discarding old ones. Entrants trained under the new content earn higher wages; older incumbents, who had completed the older curricula, see their wages fall.
authors: Anna Salomons, Cäcilia vom Baur, Ulrich Zierahn-Weilage
title: Updating what workers learn: Technology, training content, and the supply of expertise

abstract: Thermal power enterprises are major participants in China's carbon market and are central to the large-scale deployment of Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage (CCUS). This study develops a three-player dynamic evolutionary game involving the government, financial institutions, and thermal power enterprises to examine how coordinated environmental policies drive CCUS technology diffusion across the initial, transition, and mature stages of technological development. We compare three policy instruments-carbon price, green credit, and government penalties and examine how their effects on enterprises' CCUS investment decisions vary across technological stages. The results show that in the initial stage, none of the three instruments is sufficient to alter enterprises' investment strategies. In the transition stage, the effect of carbon price becomes stronger, while green credit begins to influence investment decisions. In the mature stage, carbon price plays a more prominent role in supporting CCUS investment, green credit provides financing support, and government penalties strengthen regulatory incentives. Further analysis shows that policy coordination exhibits clear stage-dependent characteristics: its effect is limited in the initial stage, most pronounced in the transition stage, and mainly accelerates convergence toward CCUS investment in the mature stage. The introduction of government penalties further strengthens this convergence effect. Furthermore, higher capture efficiency improves CCUS investment profitability under the benchmark conditions, although the negative marginal effects of initial investment and unit capture costs do not necessarily weaken. Maintaining an appropriate CO2 utilization revenue-sharing ratio between financial institutions and thermal power enterprises is particularly important during the transition stage for balancing the interests of both parties and sustaining cooperation.

abstract: Do incidental emotional shocks affect political attitudes toward state authority? We link Chinese Super League football results to respondents’ interview dates in the Chinese General Social Survey (2015, 2018, 2021, and 2023) and exploit within-province-year variation in exposure to unexpected match outcomes, classified against pre-match betting odds. Upset losses by a respondent’s provincial team increase expressed acceptance of government intervention against public criticism; the effect fades over the week after the match. The response is most pronounced in attitudes toward public criticism: parallel items on government interference in private life, social trust, and happiness show no comparable movement. These findings are consistent with transient negative emotions increasing acceptance of government control over public criticism, a reversal of the same-valence pattern documented in the political-spillover literature.

abstract: The rapid pace of digitalization and technological development has fundamentally transformed modern tax systems. Advances in information and communications technology, artificial intelligence, and data analytics are reshaping the ways in which tax administrations operate, taxpayers comply, and governments design tax policies. Against this background, the paper has three specific objectives: to review the development and implementation of tax digitalization, to examine the impact of tax digitalization on tax compliance, and to assess the impact of tax digitalization on tax complexity. As part of the first objective, the paper considers, as a case study, the World Bank’s recently launched B-READY project, which highlights the growing importance of digitalization in the operation of tax systems worldwide. The paper draws on recent developments in Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, World Bank Group, and International Monetary Fund policy reports and the academic literature. The paper offers a conceptual framework for understanding the paradox of how digital transformation simultaneously promotes efficiency and transparency and reduces operational and computational compliance burdens on the one hand, while generating new forms of administrative and regulatory complexity on the other. The paper concludes by outlining key policy implications and suggesting directions for future research on balancing technological innovation with tax simplicity and equity.

abstract: To address concerns about competitiveness and carbon leakage, countries with ambitious climate policies are increasingly looking to combine unilateral carbon pricing with border carbon adjustments. These measures aim to create a level playing field between domestically regulated energy-intensive and trade-exposed industries and their competitors abroad by imposing charges on the (unpriced) carbon embodied in imports and (potentially) rebating carbon costs on exports. At the same time, they are seen as measures that may have protectionist motivation and shift the burden of climate policy onto poorer developing economies that bear less historical responsibility for climate change, have limited financial and technological capacity for decarbonization, and may depend on carbon-intensive exports. For an informed policy debate, understanding how border carbon adjustments alter the economic burden of unilateral emissions pricing across all countries is essential. However, quantitative impact estimates derived from ex-ante simulation analyses vary considerably in the applied economic literature due to divergent assumptions on key drivers whose relative importance is difficult to distinguish from the outset. Based on controlled simulations with a large-scale computable general equilibrium model of global trade and carbon use, this paper provides a systematic sensitivity analysis of three fundamental dimensions that determine the impacts of border carbon adjustments: (i) policy design choices; (ii) the price responsiveness of supply and demand; and (iii) the input-output data characterizing initial heterogeneities of production, consumption, and trade patterns across countries.

abstract: As environmental standards become more important in cross-border trade, firms' sustainability practices increasingly shape competitiveness and market entry. Yet the relationship between energy efficiency measures (EEM) and firms' international trade participation, and the roles of productivity and certification in that relationship, remain insufficiently explored. Using World Bank Enterprise Survey data on 4865 manufacturing firms in 20 Central, Eastern, and South-Eastern European countries, this paper examines the relationship at the extensive and intensive margins of trade. EEM adoption is associated with a 5.8 percentage-point higher probability of exporting, while its association with import participation is small and statistically insignificant. The relationship is concentrated at the extensive margin, with no significant association with export intensity. A Karlson-Holm-Breen decomposition shows that international certification, rather than labour productivity, accounts for most of the indirect component. These patterns are robust to alternative definitions of EEM adoption and trade participation, to matching and weighting estimators, and to conditioning on customer environmental requirements. Although the cross-sectional design supports associations rather than causal effects, the evidence is more consistent with a supplier-qualification account, in which energy-efficiency practices and certification jointly mark firms' eligibility to supply foreign buyers, than with a productivity account.
title: Energy efficiency measures and firms' participation in international trade: Evidence from transition economies
